title: Triaxial $μ$-PIC for resolving Multi-Hit Ambiguity
summary: The micro pixel chamber ($μ$-PIC), a type of micro-pattern gaseous detectors (MPGD), features pixel electrodes structured similarly to a sliced proportional counter. Conventionally, $μ$-PIC electrodes are connected to orthogonal strip electrodes to reduce the number of readout circuits; however, this configuration introduces multi-hit ambiguity when tracing winding tracks or during high-rate operations. A well-known solution to this problem is the adoption of an additional readout axis. To this end, we designed a new electrode structure using Garfield++ simulations and fabricated a triaxial $μ$-PIC based on through-glass-via (TGV) technology. This triaxial $μ$-PIC achieved a high gas gain of $1.1\times 10^4$ and the energy resolution of 22\% (FWHM) at 5.9~keV, Furthermore, the false-hit probability was less than 0.78\% at a 95\% confidence level for two clusters separated by a distance of over 3 mm, consistent with Garfield++ predictions. With this triaxial $μ$-PIC, single avalanche signals are collected from three independent readout strip electrodes (the anode and two cathodes). The charge ratio among these electrodes remains nearly constant at anode:U-cathode:V-cathode=3:2:1. In addition, we successfully achieved an enhanced gain of $3.2\times 10^4$ without increasing the discharge risk by employing an alternative operation mode.

title: Construction and performance evaluation of a meter-scale monolithic scintillator tracker with embedded scatterers
comment: 37 pages, 17 figures. Submitted to Nuclear Instruments and Methods in Physics Research Section A
summary: A meter-scale Fiber-Readout mOnolithic and Scatterer-embedded scintillator Tracker (FROST) was constructed and operated in the NINJA experiment to enable muon-track matching between the nuclear emulsion detectors and the downstream muon detector. The detector consists of a 1.32 m $\times$ 1.40 m plastic scintillator plate assembled from optically bonded scatterer-embedded plates, with wavelength-shifting fibers arranged at a pitch of 10 mm. During J-PARC neutrino-beam operation, FROST achieved a data acquisition efficiency of 99.59% and a detection efficiency of 99.946$\pm$0.006% for selected neutrino-induced muons well within the active area. A position reconstruction method based on the light-yield distribution was developed for both single- and multi-particle events. In a neutrino-interaction simulation, muon position resolutions of 1.77 mm and 1.61 mm were achieved in the two orthogonal readout directions, assuming correct muon identification. Using a beam-data sample dominated by single-muon events, upper limits on the position resolution of 2.20 mm and 2.03 mm were obtained for track angles below 20°. These results demonstrate that the FROST concept can be scaled up to a meter-scale active area while maintaining high detection efficiency and a position resolution well below the readout pitch under actual experimental conditions.

title: Reduced-order modeling of squeeze-film damped electrostatically actuated microbeams using complex modes of the coupled problem
summary: A reduced-order model is developed for the nonlinear dynamics of electrostatically actuated microbeams, including the full squeeze film effect. The model uses Petrov-Galerkin projection on damped complex modes of the fully coupled fluid-structure problem. The Euler-Bernoulli theory for calmped-clamped and clamped-free microbeams, with mid-plane stretching and electrostatic nonlinearities, and the nonlinear compressible Reynolds equation are discretized by the differential quadrature method for the static solution and eigenvalue problem. The calculated eigenmodes are either complex conjugates describing the coupled behavior of the device or real depicting the fluid relaxation. The natural frequencies and quality factors are compared to experimental and numerical results found in the literature. Depending on the ambient pressure, the geometry of the microbeam, and the fluid boundary conditions, squeeze-film effect can impact not only the effective damping of the device but also its dynamics. It is shown that in some cases dropping fluid relaxation modes cannot be compensated by any set of purely structural modes. The non-classical damping introduced by the fluid modes is a spatially distributed phase difference between pressure and deflection. The convergence analysis of the dynamic response resulting from the reduced-order model showed that a basis with one set of coupled modes and one fluid mode can reproduce the results of a fully discretized model within 1.5% error and at much faster computational time.

title: Reliability of Fisher-information bounds for dielectric metalenses: a site-resolved RCWA audit
summary: We assess the reliability of localization precision predicted for a 1716-nanopillar dielectric metalens using a site-resolved complex RCWA library and a vectorial Poisson Fisher model. An independent calculation reproduces the archived local axial Cramer-Rao bound of 20.7738 nm to within 0.0044 nm, yielding 20.7695 nm under the same ideal detector and 3000 detected signal photons. High-order periodic-cell calculations reveal a 0.1335 rad phase difference at a selected diameter; different substrate-index assumptions prevent attributing this difference solely to modal truncation. Replacing the recalculated coefficients at 39 actual sites changes the bound to 20.7522 nm. Restricted phase-mask benchmarks and pixel-integration checks further distinguish a stable statistical prediction from electromagnetic convergence. We provide a reproducible, model-conditional benchmark, not a physical-device performance claim.

title: Task-Aware Bitrate Thresholds for Codec-Robust Ultrasound Segmentation
comment: It is already accepted at IEEE Visual Communications and Image Processing Conference
summary: Remote robot surgery and tele-ultrasound increasingly rely on real-time streaming under strict bandwidth constraints, making lossy compression unavoidable. Since the receiving end of these clinical pipelines is increasingly a machine rather than a human observer, codec selection must be guided by downstream task accuracy rather than perceptual fidelity. We evaluate three widely deployed codecs, H.264/AVC, HEVC, and AV1, on prostate ultrasound segmentation, reporting task-aware compression performance with region overlap (Dice) and boundary accuracy (HD95) as the quality metrics. To compare codecs fairly, we match their operating points at a common perceptual-quality (SSIM) level. We establish, per codec, the lowest bitrate that preserves acceptable segmentation accuracy, reporting the 5th-percentile Dice alongside the mean to expose worst-case degradation. All three codecs preserve segmentation quality (mean Dice $\geq$ 0.84) down to approximately 0.07-0.20 bits per voxel (bpv). Below this point, AV1's accuracy declines gradually, while H.264's drops sharply. As a result, H.264 needs 82% more bitrate than AV1 to reach the same region-overlap accuracy (Dice), and 104.7% more to reach the same boundary accuracy (HD95).

title: Laser fabrication of vibrating microcavities on silicon: Formation dynamics and frequency tunability
summary: Laser processing of silicon has long since become a standard method for wafer dicing, surface texturing, re-crystallization after ion implantation, as well as surface amorphization, to name a few examples. Here, we introduce a novel concept, the fabrication of vibrating microcavities in a commercial platform, Si wafers covered by a thick SiO2 layer, acting as a membrane. We demonstrate that by exposing our material system to single ultrashort laser pulses above the evaporation threshold of Si, a controlled delamination of the cover layer without fracture can be achieved, leading to the formation of a microcavity accompanied by a surface bulging up to 1.5 micrometer. The formation dynamics of the microcavities has been investigated by time-resolved optical probe techniques. Ultrafast pump-probe microscopy resolves the initial stages of substrate melting, the onset of layer expansion followed by relaxation. Real-time reflectivity measurements with nanosecond resolution resolve the long lived, highly complex oscillation process of the membrane, extending over tens of microseconds. The formed cavities can be re-excited at low fluence without damage or degradation, featuring vibrations at single frequencies with high Q factors. The frequencies can be tuned continuously from 8 MHz up to 19 MHz by adjusting the fabrication fluence. A simple classical model is found to well describe the behavior of the membranes. Our results pave the way for applications in micro- and nanooptics and acoustics, in great part due to the commercial availability of the Si-SiO2 platform and the simplicity of the fabrication method. An extension to the field of microelectromechanical system (MEMS) of this technology is proposed.

title: Dispersive Corrections to Electromagnetic Energy and Power Flux Are Imprints of Eliminated Degrees of Freedom
summary: In a spatially dispersive medium the electromagnetic energy and flux are given by the frequency and wave-vector derivatives of the constitutive parameters, a result known as the Agranovich--Ginzburg (AG) formulas. Here, we clarify the physical meaning of the derivative terms in these relations and show that they measure the energy and flux carried by the degrees of freedom of the internal field-matter dynamics that the Maxwellian constitutive description hides. We construct an extended state-space model of such dynamics for a wide class of temporally and spatially dispersive media, from which the Maxwellian constitutive relations follow upon elimination of the internal variables, the effective material operator resulting from the Schur complement of the eliminated internal block. A congruence identity relates this complement to the extended state-space description, which allows us to extend the AG formulas to general bianisotropic media and to establish the conditions of their validity in the presence of dissipation. The AG dispersive corrections are thus the imprints of the eliminated degrees of freedom rather than independent constitutive postulates. They hold for fields driven at arbitrary real frequency and wave vector, and not only for eigenmodes, provided that the sources act on the fields alone and that any dissipation is carried by the electromagnetic subsystem. We verify the construction on the Lorentz, Drude, magnetized-plasma, and hydrodynamic models, the last of which describes a nonlocal metal. Additionally, a capacitively loaded wire medium is treated in the Supplemental Material.

title: Finite Element Elastographic Analysis of Kidney MRI for Computational Assessment of Chronic Kidney Disease
summary:
Background and Objective: Bridging kidney MRI with patient-specific computational biomechanics may enable accurate, noninvasive assessment of chronic kidney disease. To develop a finite element method (FEM)-based computational elastography framework for estimating renal biomechanical properties from conventional kidney MRI and to evaluate its ability to differentiate chronic kidney disease (CKD) from healthy controls.
  Methods: Kidney segmentation masks from healthy control and CKD subjects were converted into triangulated surface meshes, and watertight surfaces were tetrahedralized to create volumetric FEM meshes. Kidney tissue was modeled as a nearly incompressible Kelvin-Voigt viscoelastic material. Harmonic wave propagation simulations were performed using FEM, followed by Helmholtz-based elastographic inversion to estimate complex shear modulus distributions. Derived biomechanical parameters were used for CKD classification using machine learning models.
  Results: FEM-derived stiffness estimates showed consistency with stiffness ranges previously reported in human renal MRE studies and also showed measurable differences between healthy and CKD groups. Machine learning models trained on FEM-derived features achieved classification performance up to 86.26% cross-validation accuracy with an AUC of 0.92.
  Conclusion: FEM-derived elastographic parameters showed potential for distinguishing CKD from healthy tissue and may provide an alternative for renal biomechanical assessment without dedicated MRE acquisition.

title: A nonlinear interface for phase transduction
summary: Broadband nonlinear frequency conversion mixes multiple input frequencies, complicating the transfer of programmed spectral phase between widely separated spectral bands. Here we identify and experimentally realize a quasi-linear phase-transduction regime enabled by broad phase-matching acceptance and effective localization of the complex frequency-mixing response. This selectivity can arise from coherent interference without narrowing the pump spectrum. We implement this regime through dispersive four-wave mixing in an argon-filled hollow-capillary fiber, transferring spectral phase from 1032-nm near-infrared signals to 344-nm ultraviolet idlers. Transient-grating frequency-resolved optical gating reveals frequency-inverted, phase-conjugating transfer of quadratic dispersion, localized phase steps, and low-frequency sinusoidal modulation. After correction for the modeled pump-induced phase background, the quadratic and step responses exhibit approximately linear point-by-point correlations. With increasing pump chirp, the transferred phase steps become more sharply preserved, and the fitted phase-transfer gains approach unity, consistent with enhanced effective localization. These results demonstrate quasi-linear spectral-phase transduction in a co-propagating broadband nonlinear interaction without spatially separating its spectral components.

title: Simulation of Refraction Through Voxel Volumes
summary: Ray tracing in X-ray science has typically been limited to descriptions where refraction occurs only at interfaces, ignoring the refraction occurring due to the continuous variations in index of refraction in the bulk of a material, as are common in biological samples like bone. We propose a method to simulate X-ray images directly on voxel grids using curved rays. We first validate this method compared to a model with an analytical solution, and then investigate the effects of voxel size, interpolation choice, and illumination to grid alignment on a few simulated test objects. From these investigations, we make several recommendations to guide simulations using these techniques.

title: Stable dissipative topological solitons in media with even-order dispersion
comment: 12 pages, 7 figures, to be published in Optics Express
summary: The formation and dynamics of dissipative solitons are governed by the interplay of dispersion and nonlinearity, alongside the gain-loss balance. While it is known that dispersion orders beyond the conventional second order support stable solitons, the possibility of the creation of dissipative topological solitons in this setting was not explored. Here, we reveal a class of stable dissipative solitons enabled by the pure-high-even-order dispersion (PHEOD), with dispersion orders m=4, 6, 8, and 10. The resulting dissipative topological solitons (DTSs) and moving topological solitons (MTSs) are dark-type structures featuring a zero-amplitude point that separates two CW backgrounds with opposite signs. In particular, the PHEOD solitons feature oscillatory tails, which are not present in the conventional dark states. The linear-stability analysis confirms full robustness of the PHEOD-supported DTSs and MTSs. We also explore collision dynamics of MTSs, whose repulsive interactions are inelastic, leading either to rebound, accompanied by emission of dispersive radiation, or complete fusion. These findings establish PHEOD as a means for the generation of new species of dissipative solitons, and broaden the variety of nonlinear modes available to experimental studies in nonlinear optics.

title: Experimental demonstration of dual-polarization nonreciprocal thermal emission at moderate magnetic fields
summary: Conventional thermal emitters obey Kirchhoff's law of thermal radiation, which requires emissivity and absorptivity to be equal at each wavelength, angle, and polarization. This in turn places a fundamental limit on a range of radiative energy technologies as well as heat transfer. This constraint can however be overcome using magneto-optic semiconductors, which break Lorentz reciprocity under an applied magnetic field. However, in most prior experimental demonstrations, nonreciprocity has been restricted to TM polarization, since the electric field of TE-polarized light is parallel to the applied magnetic field. Here, we experimentally demonstrate nonreciprocal absorption in both polarizations at the same wavelengths and angles from a single structure, wherein a germanium Mie-resonant metasurface on a doped InAs layer scatters TE-polarized light into near fields with components perpendicular to the magnetic field, allowing the magneto-optic response of the InAs to act on them. Under a 0.48 T field from a permanent Halbach array, this structure exhibits a difference in absorptivity between $+B$ and $-B$ of 0.035 in both TE and TM polarization at 16.6 $μ$m. Our approach shows that the magneto-optic response of a planar semiconductor and the resonances of a dielectric metasurface can be designed together, offering a potential route to dual-polarization nonreciprocity at fields available from permanent magnets for emerging energy and heat transfer technologies.

title: Simulation of Refraction Through Voxel Volumes
summary: Ray tracing in X-ray science has typically been limited to descriptions where refraction occurs only at interfaces, ignoring the refraction occurring due to the continuous variations in index of refraction in the bulk of a material, as are common in biological samples like bone. We propose a method to simulate X-ray images directly on voxel grids using curved rays. We first validate this method compared to a model with an analytical solution, and then investigate the effects of voxel size, interpolation choice, and illumination to grid alignment on a few simulated test objects. From these investigations, we make several recommendations to guide simulations using these techniques.

title: Unified design of short mode-evolution couplers
summary: Short mode-evolution couplers have been designed with several seemingly different approaches, including fast quasi-adiabatic dynamics (FAQUAD), counter-diabatic (CD) driving realized by tailoring waveguide widths and spacing, CD driving realized by axis bending, and numerical optimization of the coupler geometry. Using exact two-mode coupled-mode theory in the Kramers--Henneberger frame of the bent coupler, we show that these approaches belong to the same design space. The three geometric parameters, width difference, spacing, and axis tilt, act on the light through two functions only: the coupling strength, set by the spacing, and an effective detuning, set by the width difference and the axis curvature. The gauge, bent, and mixed realizations of a CD coupler are therefore the same device and have the same bandwidth. The bandwidth is set by the angle $χ$ between the light and the field that steers it on the Bloch sphere, integrated along the device as $\int\sin^2χdz$, and for a CD coupler this integral is set by the reference alone. This leads to a lithography-aware design rule: make the reference as adiabatic as the minimum gap allows, by narrowing its spacing at the anticrossing, and let exact CD suppress the remaining nonadiabatic coupling. In beam propagation method (BPM) simulations on a polymer platform, a 500\um{} coupler designed this way, without numerical optimization, maintains ${>}99\%$ transfer over 274~nm at a minimum edge gap of 1.05\um, compared with 150~nm for the CD coupler of a fixed-spacing reference at nearly the same gap. Particle swarm optimization of the geometry with BPM in the loop does not exceed the design rule. Three-dimensional BPM of the BCB channel waveguides also confirms these conclusions.

title: Laser fabrication of vibrating microcavities on silicon: Formation dynamics and frequency tunability
summary: Laser processing of silicon has long since become a standard method for wafer dicing, surface texturing, re-crystallization after ion implantation, as well as surface amorphization, to name a few examples. Here, we introduce a novel concept, the fabrication of vibrating microcavities in a commercial platform, Si wafers covered by a thick SiO2 layer, acting as a membrane. We demonstrate that by exposing our material system to single ultrashort laser pulses above the evaporation threshold of Si, a controlled delamination of the cover layer without fracture can be achieved, leading to the formation of a microcavity accompanied by a surface bulging up to 1.5 micrometer. The formation dynamics of the microcavities has been investigated by time-resolved optical probe techniques. Ultrafast pump-probe microscopy resolves the initial stages of substrate melting, the onset of layer expansion followed by relaxation. Real-time reflectivity measurements with nanosecond resolution resolve the long lived, highly complex oscillation process of the membrane, extending over tens of microseconds. The formed cavities can be re-excited at low fluence without damage or degradation, featuring vibrations at single frequencies with high Q factors. The frequencies can be tuned continuously from 8 MHz up to 19 MHz by adjusting the fabrication fluence. A simple classical model is found to well describe the behavior of the membranes. Our results pave the way for applications in micro- and nanooptics and acoustics, in great part due to the commercial availability of the Si-SiO2 platform and the simplicity of the fabrication method. title: Continuum Photonic Axion Insulators
summary: Here, I study the conditions for realizing an axion topology in a homogeneous inversion-symmetric electromagnetic continuum, in the absence of a crystalline lattice. I introduce a continuum inversion invariant expressed solely in terms of the spectral properties of the material response in the zero- and infinite-wave-vector limits. Surprisingly, it is found that standard gyrotropic-type material responses are strongly constrained and, under fairly general conditions, cannot open an axion gap within first-order perturbation theory. Based on an analogy between the effective response of crystalline photonic axion insulators and the optical response of centrosymmetric altermagnets, a class of spatially dispersive odd magnetoelectric couplings that can open an axion gap is identified. These findings suggest an interesting hierarchy of nonreciprocal mechanisms in electromagnetic continua: while uniform gyrotropy relates to Chern phases, odd magnetoelectric coupling relates to axion phases.

title: A Passive Intelligent Metasurface: A Network Model
summary: Intelligent metasurfaces enable advanced wave manipulation, including negative refraction, focusing, beam splitting and beam steering, with significant potential for practical applications. However, conventional approaches often rely on active metamaterials with gain, or demand computationally intensive solutions of inverse problems to find the optimal configuration. In this work, we use the scattering framework of quantum graph theory to derive an exact, analytic expression for configuration of a passive metasurface that produces a prescribed reflected wave field. The metasurface terminates a periodic lattice of waveguides and consists of an array of channels, each a tube of length $\ell_m$ ending in a vertex whose scattering parameter $λ_m$ sets how much of the wave is lost to the wall. For any prescribed incident and reflected field, the exact lengths and scattering parameters follow channel by channel, in closed form, from the ratio of the wave amplitudes returning to and leaving the lattice, and the metasurface is passive whenever this ratio does not exceed unity in modulus. We demonstrate the construction for both a one-dimensional and a two-dimensional metasurface. The one-dimensional metasurface terminates a two-dimensional lattice and steers, splits or perfectly absorbs Gaussian beams. The two-dimensional metasurface terminates a three-dimensional lattice and generates a prescribed image in a plane inside the lattice. In each case, we obtain the exact boundary properties that produce the effect.

title: Hybrid integration of a SESAM with a silicon nitride photonic integrated circuit
summary: The realization of high-performance femtosecond lasers on photonic integrated circuits (PICs) requires robust, low-loss coupling between a saturable absorber and a photonic waveguide. In this work, we demonstrate the hybrid integration of a semiconductor saturable absorber mirror (SESAM) with a silicon nitride (SiN) PIC by micro-assembly. This micro-assembly strategy transfers the non-linear functionality of the absorber onto the PIC. We characterize the linear and non-linear performance of an unbonded SESAM and of a SESAM bonded to inverse-tapered SiN waveguides. At 1560~nm, the bonded device shows a waveguide-coupled modulation depth of 5.2\%, a maximum reflectivity of 37.2\%, and a saturation fluence of 47~\textmu J/cm$^2$. This work demonstrates that SESAMs can be integrated directly onto silicon nitride-based PIC platforms and provides a pathway towards fully integrated, self-starting, chip-scale ultrafast lasers.

title: Thermal Inverse Design: Tailoring the Transient Response of Resistive Micro-Heaters
summary: Microheaters underpin a broad range of applications that require localized and dynamic thermal control. Engineering their spatial and temporal temperature distributions is therefore essential, yet conventional heater design relies largely on iterative trial and error involving numerous full-scale thermal simulations. Here, we introduce an inverse design algorithm for pulsed heating, a common operating modality in thermal processing, sensing, switching, and material characterization. The approach uses a single lithographic step to pattern the doped regions of a silicon microheater and, in principle, enables on-demand peak temperature distributions under transient voltage excitation within one closed design loop. The algorithm also incorporates practical fabrication constraints, including finite lithographic resolution. We demonstrate its versatility through three representative designs. First, an optimized heater achieves more than a 20-fold reduction in temperature nonuniformity compared with a conventional uniformly doped heater. Second, inverse-designed doping effectively cancels the thermal gradient in a heater connected in series with a diode. Third, the method generates prescribed linear temperature gradients on demand. These results establish inverse-designed doping as a scalable and fabrication-compatible approach for tailoring transient temperature distributions in resistive microheaters.

title: Photonic Exceptional Topological Bound States in the Continuum
summary: Exceptional bound states in the continuum (EBICs) arise when bound states in the continuum (BICs) with distinct intrinsic losses coalesce at exceptional points (EPs), combining continuum-embedded wave confinement with a non-analytic spectral response. However, conventional EBICs rely on precisely controlled modal coupling and intrinsic loss, making them fragile and difficult to realize experimentally. Here, we introduce bulk-band topology to mitigate this fragility and experimentally realize a photonic exceptional topological BIC (ETBIC) in spoof surface plasmon polariton waveguides by merging two symmetry-protected topological BICs (TBICs) to coalesce at an EP, with the topological design supporting robust localization under symmetry-preserving perturbations. By engineering an intrinsic loss contrast and tuning the intermodal coupling, we directly resolve the coalescence of the complex eigenfrequencies, accompanied by measured near-field distributions consistent with the exceptional eigenstate. Furthermore, weak perturbations induce approximately square-root eigenfrequency splitting, yielding an enhanced spectral response compared with the approximately linear frequency shift of an isolated TBIC. These results establish bulk-band topology as a design principle for exceptional BIC engineering and provide a foundation for EBIC-based photonic sensing.

title: Characterization and Suppression of Parasitic Back-Reflection Noise in Transponder-Type Heterodyne Interferometry
summary: Transponder-type heterodyne interferometry is a versatile metrological technique for high-precision measurements, with applications in Earth's gravity-field recovery, space-based gravitational-wave detection, deep-space ranging, and Doppler tracking. However, parasitic back-reflections can contaminate phase readout and degrade measurement sensitivity. To characterize and suppress this noise, we constructed a transponder-type interferometer with coaxially aligned counter-propagating beams, achieving stable operation at a received optical power of 720 pW. An adjustable reflecting system was introduced into the master-side transmit path to simulate back-reflection under realistic conditions. Optical path scans and model fitting showed that phase errors vary periodically with the relative phase between the main and parasitic interference signals, which defines the working point. Assisted by π measurement, adjustment to low-sensitivity working points was combined with balanced detection to suppress back-reflection phase noise, achieving maximum suppression factors of 77 for single-frequency phase errors and 23 for band-limited phase-noise amplitude spectral density. π measurement also enabled working point diagnosis at 3.8 nW back-reflection power, confirming its applicability under weak back-reflection conditions. These results provide an effective approach for in situ back-reflection characterization and phase-noise suppression in transponder-type heterodyne interferometry.

title: Goos-Hänchen Shifts at 458 nm from DUV Dichroic Laser Mirrors
summary: We report polarization- and angle-dependent lateral beam shifts observed at 458~nm upon reflection from a deep-ultraviolet (DUV) dichroic multilayer mirror. These Goos--Hänchen (GH) shifts originate from the phase of the complex Fresnel reflection coefficient and are quantitatively reproduced using a transfer-matrix model. Simultaneous reflectance (R), transmittance (T), and GH shift measurements provide complementary constraints on the coating's amplitude and phase response. The analysis is extended to transmission, predicting analogous phase-induced lateral shifts. In frequency-doubling cavities using dichroic mirrors, these phase effects can accumulate over multiple reflections, leading to deviations from ray-optics predictions that may affect cavity mode structure and resonance conditions. Our results show a GH shift of as much as 2~\textmu m (\bm{$\approx 4.4λ$}), which, combined with RT data, enables improved characterization of the phase response of the multilayer coating. The p-polarized reflectance is minimized at a pseudo-Brewster angle of \bm{$θ_B \approx 46^\circ$} at 458~nm, providing a natural reference point around which the GH shift is enhanced.

title: An Agent-Driven, Cross-Validated Inverse-Design Pipeline for Dielectric Metasurfaces
comment: The code, are openly available on GitHub at \url{https://github.com/GiuseppeELio/metasurface-agent-pipeline} (MIT License) and archived on Zenodo at 10.5281/zenodo.23982523
summary: Inverse design of dielectric metasurfaces is powerful but labour-intensive: each new target requires choosing a parameterization and a figure of merit, managing compute resources, and critically assessing results that may be numerically unconverged, sensitive to fabrication errors or trapped in local optima. Here we present an open-source pipeline in which an artificial intelligence (AI) coding agent turns a plain-language specification into metasurface optimization runs, executes them, analyses every run with a fixed checklist and proposes the next iteration. Designs are optimized with differentiable three-dimensional rigorous coupled-wave analysis (RCWA), including robustness to fabrication tolerances, and every reported design is independently verified with finite-difference time-domain (FDTD) simulations. We demonstrate the workflow at 1550 nm on a freeform silicon metagrating, on a polarization-independent meta-atom library assembled into beam-deflecting supercells, and on metalenses built from the same library. In the metagrating case, the independent FDTD verification revealed a 5\% overestimate of the efficiency by the optimization model that a conventional convergence test had not detected, and the robust design retained most of its efficiency under $\pm$10~nm fabrication errors. In the other cases, instead, the obtained RCWA results are confirmed by full-wave simulations.

title: Analytical Modeling of the Admittance Tensor of Periodic Elliptical Meta-Atoms
summary: A metasurface is an electrically thin interface that controls the phase, amplitude and polarization of a wave, upon reflection or transmission. Printed on a grounded dielectric substrate and spatially modulated across the aperture, it converts a guided surface wave into a radiated leaky wave, a mechanism used in holographic metasurface antennas. Controlling this conversion requires synthesizing a prescribed distribution of admittance tensors, each derived from the homogenization of a subwavelength unit cell. Many numerical and semi-analytical methods have been proposed to relate the geometry of a meta-atom to the tensor it produces. This paper presents, to the author's knowledge, the first analytical model, restricted to elliptical meta-atoms on a uniform lattice. The Galerkin method is applied directly to the geometry of the patches, without spatial meshing. An affine transformation maps any rotated ellipse onto the unit disk, so that a single formulation covers every configuration. A wideband response takes from minutes to tens of minutes with a periodic full-wave solver, while the proposed model evaluates it in a few tens of milliseconds on the same workstation, roughly three orders of magnitude faster. The predicted admittance agrees with a method-of-moments reference up to the fundamental resonance and captures the guided-mode anomaly of the substrate. Beyond the physical insight it brings, the model is a differentiable function of the geometry, which makes the quasi-real-time design of optimized metasurfaces possible.

title: Machine learning classification of dynamical phases in a driven nonlinear Su-Schrieffer-Heeger lattice
comment: 13 pages, 7 figures (3 in the main text, 4 in the appendices)
summary: Driven nonlinear photonic lattices can settle into steady, symmetry-broken, periodic, or chaotic states, and mapping where each occurs in parameter space is key to device design. Brute-force mapping is slow and relies on hand-built criteria, while machine-learning classifiers are usually tested on different systems, so it is unclear which suits a new lattice. We therefore apply four classifiers to the same coherently driven Su-Schrieffer-Heeger (SSH) chain of Kerr resonators: a hand-built heuristic classifier based on Lyapunov exponents and spectral diagnostics, a supervised convolutional neural network (CNN) trained on the heuristic labels, an unsupervised library-building scheme based on augmented dynamic mode decomposition (aDMD), and an unsupervised Gaussian mixture model (GMM) on four dynamical invariants that include an aDMD reconstruction error. Using a converged heuristic diagram as the reference, the CNN reaches 98.0% held-out accuracy, while the two label-free methods reach adjusted Rand indices (ARIs) of 0.916 and 0.947, respectively, without seeing any labels. We show that the aDMD library cleanly resolves the stable and bistable phases and separates symmetric from symmetry-broken periodic oscillations, which the heuristic misses, though it cannot distinguish periodic from chaotic switching. We also find that a poorly converged reference understates the label-free methods' accuracy.

title: Reprogrammable polaritonic skyrmion and meron lattices based on the phase-change material In$_3$SbTe$_2$
summary: Optical topological quasiparticles such as skyrmions and merons consist of engineered electromagnetic fields which can be realized via the controlled interference of polaritons. The resulting polaritonic topological lattices offer a promising platform for on-chip information encoding and nanoscale light-matter interaction. However, realizing these functionalities requires active tailoring of the polaritonic topological lattice. Although previous works have achieved tuning of the size of the polaritonic lattice sites, these methods relied on cumbersome and time-consuming fabrication processes and do not allow reconfiguration of the topological invariant. Here, we demonstrate fast optical prototyping of reconfigurable hexagonal and square coupling structures for the generation of polaritonic topological lattices with hyperbolic phonon polaritons in hBN using the phase-change material In$_3$SbTe$_2$. As In$_3$SbTe$_2$ can be switched reversibly between its dielectric ($\varepsilon$>0) amorphous and metallic ($\varepsilon$<0) crystalline phase by laser pulses, metallic In$_3$SbTe$_2$ coupling structures can be optically programmed and reconfigured. Our approach enables tailoring the size of the topological lattice sites by tuning the incident frequency. Moreover, In$_3$SbTe$_2$ allows for tailoring the topological invariant by reprogramming the coupling structure. Our platform enables reprogramming of robust optical topologies within minutes, opening a route toward rewritable on-chip photonic computing based on robust and on demand reconfigurable topological states.

title: Deep-learning surrogate model for rapid quantum-noise computation in dual-pump fiber-optic phase-sensitive amplifiers
summary: Fiber-optic parametric amplifiers in a phase-sensitive amplifier (PSA) configuration are well known for their low noise properties. Quantum mechanics dictates that these amplifiers can have a 0 dB noise figure (NF) (ratio of signal-to-noise ratio at the input and output of the amplifier) under certain conditions. However, for a dual-pump configuration, when the system is highly nonlinear, fully quantum calculations of NF become non-trivial. In such cases, semi-quantum models of NF evaluation exists, however, they are often complicated and resource intensive. To simplify that, in this work, first we use a semi-quantum NF calculation framework for the generation of numerically simulated input-output dataset of NF over a large parameter spaces. Then we use the data to train an optimized deep neural network (DNN) for rapid NF prediction. Utilizing the DNN, we demonstrate about 400 times reduction in the computation time compared to the standard semi-quantum NF evaluation approach with a mean absolute error (MAE) of 0.0015 dB. Using clustering we demonstrate a rapid exploration of the parameter space with respect to high gain (20 dB) and low NF (0.3 dB) targets and retrieve associated design parameters. These results illustrate the efficacy of machine learning-based approaches for rapid search of high-dimensional parameter spaces especially in compute intensive photonic systems.
